Activity: Avoid strenuous activity until reviewed by the treating team.

Warning signs: Contact the surgical team for spreading redness, pus, wound opening, or fever.

Admission date: 09 Dec 2025 | Discharge date: 21 Dec 2025
Admission diagnosis: upper gastrointestinal bleeding

A. Brief Hospital Course
The patient was admitted on 09 Dec 2025 with melena, dizziness, and symptomatic anaemia. Initial assessment showed Hb low; endoscopy showed a bleeding gastric ulcer treated endoscopically. The working diagnosis was upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Investigations and clinical monitoring were performed. Treatment included IV proton-pump inhibitor, fluids, one unit packed red cells, and endoscopic haemostasis. The patient responded to treatment and at discharge on 21 Dec 2025 was no further melena; haemoglobin stable on repeat testing. See medication reconciliation for the complete list.

Discharge diagnosis: upper GI bleed due to gastric ulcer

B. Discharge Instructions
Discharge medications: Pantoprazole 40 mg, twice daily before meals, for 8 weeks. Ferrous sulfate 325 mg, once daily, for 30 days.
Diet: Resume a regular diet as tolerated; maintain hydration.
Activity: No heavy lifting (over 5 kg) for 2 weeks. Short walks are encouraged.
Wound care: Check the wound daily for increasing redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, or separation. Showering is permitted; pat dry.
Rehabilitation: No formal rehabilitation arranged; gradually return to baseline activity.
Follow-up: See Neurology / TIA clinic in within 2 weeks; appointment date not documented.
Pending investigations: No pending investigations documented.
Warning signs: Seek immediate help for black stools, vomiting blood, or dizziness/fainting.
Additional note: Take one tablet regularly. (Drug, strength, and timing not stated.)

The patient was admitted on 18 Oct 2025 with fever, flank pain, dysuria, and vomiting. Initial assessment showed urinalysis with pyuria; urine culture grew susceptible E. coli. The working diagnosis was acute pyelonephritis. Investigations and clinical monitoring were performed. Treatment included IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesia, then oral antibiotics. The patient responded to treatment and at discharge on 30 Oct 2025 was afebrile, tolerating oral intake, and pain improved. VS stable; tolerating PO and mobilising independently.

Discharge diagnosis: acute pyelonephritis

B. Discharge Instructions
Meds on discharge: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg, BD, for 5 days. Paracetamol 650 mg, SOS for fever/pain, for as needed. Acetaminophen 500 mg, q6h PRN, for 5 days.
Diet: Drink adequate fluids unless otherwise restricted.
Activity: Walk as tolerated; increase activity gradually. Avoid strenuous exercise for 1 week.
Wound care: Keep the incision clean and dry. Remove the outer dressing after 24 hours; do not soak the wound until reviewed.
Rehabilitation: Use the incentive spirometer 10 times every hour while awake and continue walking daily.
Follow-up: Follow up with Primary care; appointment date to be confirmed. Please call the clinic.
Pending investigations: Repeat CBC in 1 week; order provided.
Warning signs: Seek urgent care for chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, confusion, or new weakness.

The patient was admitted on 31 Aug 2026 with right upper-quadrant pain, fever, and vomiting. Initial assessment showed ultrasound showed gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid. The working diagnosis was acute cholecystitis. Investigations and clinical monitoring were performed. Treatment included IV fluids, antibiotics, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The patient responded to treatment and at discharge on 09 Sep 2026 was recovering well, tolerating low-fat diet, and mobilising.

Discharge diagnosis: acute calculous cholecystitis, status post laparoscopic cholecystectomy

Amoxicillin-clavulanate 625 mg — TDS — duration 5 days. Paracetamol 500 mg — 1–2 tablets every 6 hours PRN — duration 3 days.
Diet: Choose a low-fat diet for the next 2 weeks, then advance as tolerated.
Activity: No heavy lifting (over 5 kg) for 2 weeks. Short walks are encouraged.
Wound care: No wound care required.
Rehabilitation: No formal rehabilitation arranged; gradually return to baseline activity.
Follow-up: Appointment: 28 Sep 2026 with Cardiology.
Pending investigations: Biopsy pathology report pending; discuss results at surgical follow-up.
Warning signs: Seek immediate help for black stools, vomiting blood, or dizziness/fainting.

Activity: Rest today and gradually return to normal activity over 3–5 days.
Wound care: Check the wound daily for increasing redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, or separation. Showering is permitted; pat dry.

Admission date: 26 Apr 2026 | Discharge date: 30 Apr 2026
Admission diagnosis: upper gastrointestinal bleeding

A. Brief Hospital Course
The patient was admitted on 26 Apr 2026 with melena, dizziness, and symptomatic anaemia. Initial assessment showed Hb low; endoscopy showed a bleeding gastric ulcer treated endoscopically. The working diagnosis was upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Investigations and clinical monitoring were performed. Treatment included IV proton-pump inhibitor, fluids, one unit packed red cells, and endoscopic haemostasis. The patient responded to treatment and at discharge on 30 Apr 2026 was no further melena; haemoglobin stable on repeat testing. See medication reconciliation for the complete list.

Discharge diagnosis: upper GI bleed due to gastric ulcer

B. Discharge Instructions
Discharge medications: Pantoprazole 40 mg, twice daily before meals, for 8 weeks. Ferrous sulfate 325 mg, once daily, for 30 days. Docusate 100 mg, twice daily, for 7 days.
Diet: Resume a regular diet as tolerated; maintain hydration.
Activity: Walk as tolerated; increase activity gradually. Avoid strenuous exercise for 1 week.
Wound care: Check the wound daily for increasing redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, or separation. Showering is permitted; pat dry.
Rehabilitation: Use the incentive spirometer 10 times every hour while awake and continue walking daily.
Follow-up: Follow up with Neurology / TIA clinic; appointment date to be confirmed. Please call the clinic.
Pending investigations: No pending investigations documented.
Warning signs: Seek urgent care for chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, confusion, or new weakness.

A. Brief Hospital Course
The patient was admitted on 23 Jun 2026 with melena, dizziness, and symptomatic anaemia. Initial assessment showed Hb low; endoscopy showed a bleeding gastric ulcer treated endoscopically. The working diagnosis was upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Investigations and clinical monitoring were performed. Treatment included IV proton-pump inhibitor, fluids, one unit packed red cells, and endoscopic haemostasis. The patient responded to treatment and at discharge on 24 Jun 2026 was no further melena; haemoglobin stable on repeat testing. See medication reconciliation for the complete list.

Discharge diagnosis: upper GI bleed due to gastric ulcer

B. Discharge Instructions
Discharge medications: Pantoprazole 40 mg, twice daily before meals, for 8 weeks. Ferrous sulfate 325 mg, once daily, for 30 days. Ondansetron 4 mg, every 8 hours as needed, for 3 days.
Diet: Resume a regular diet as tolerated; maintain hydration.
Activity: Rest today and gradually return to normal activity over 3–5 days.
Wound care: Check the wound daily for increasing redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, or separation. Showering is permitted; pat dry.
Rehabilitation: No formal rehabilitation arranged; gradually return to baseline activity.
Follow-up: Appointment: 14 Jul 2026 with General Surgery.
Pending investigations: No pending investigations documented.
Warning signs: Call emergency services for facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty, or sudden vision loss.

The patient was admitted on 19 May 2025 with acute flank pain radiating to groin with nausea. Initial assessment showed CT KUB showed a 4 mm distal ureteric calculus; renal function stable. The working diagnosis was renal colic. Investigations and clinical monitoring were performed. Treatment included IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetic, and medical expulsive therapy. The patient responded to treatment and at discharge on 23 May 2025 was pain controlled and able to drink fluids. VS stable; tolerating PO and mobilising independently.

Discharge diagnosis: ureteric calculus with renal colic

Medication list: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg, at night, for 14 days. Naproxen 250 mg, q12h with food as needed, for 5 days. Acetaminophen 500 mg, q6h PRN, for 5 days. Take as directed.
Diet: Take small, frequent meals; avoid alcohol, NSAIDs, and foods that worsen gastric symptoms.
Activity: Rest today and gradually return to normal activity over 3–5 days.
Wound care: Keep the incision clean and dry. Remove the outer dressing after 24 hours; do not soak the wound until reviewed.
Rehabilitation: No formal rehabilitation arranged; gradually return to baseline activity.
Follow-up: Appointment: 05 Jun 2025 with Wound clinic.
Pending investigations: Outpatient echocardiogram requested; appointment date not yet assigned.
Warning signs: Call emergency services for facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty, or sudden vision loss.
